summary: Furosemide is a potent loop diuretic used to treat edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome), and to treat hypertension. It blocks sodium-chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle, producing a rapid, high-ceiling diuresis with onset within 1 hour orally and within minutes intravenously. Because it can cause profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion, dosing must be individualized with careful medical supervision. It carries a boxed warning for ototoxicity (tinnitus and reversible or irreversible hearing loss), particularly with rapid IV injection, high doses, renal impairment, hypoproteinemia, or concurrent ototoxic drugs. As a sulfonamide-derivative, patients allergic to sulfonamides may also react to furosemide.
indications: Edema associated with congestive heart failure (adults and pediatric patients)
Edema associated with hepatic cirrhosis (adults and pediatric patients)
Edema associated with renal disease, including the nephrotic syndrome (adults and pediatric patients)
Hypertension in adults, alone or combined with other antihypertensive agents

moa: Furosemide is a high-ceiling loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, blocking reabsorption of sodium and chloride primarily in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, and also in the proximal and distal tubules. Its high efficacy derives from this unique site of action, and its effect is independent of carbonic anhydrase inhibition and of aldosterone. The resulting natriuresis and water loss reduce extracellular fluid volume and venous return, relieving edema and lowering blood pressure. Increased delivery of sodium to the distal nephron drives potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, accounting for hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, and calcium and magnesium excretion are also increased.

relative: Hepatic coma or severe electrolyte depletion (correct before starting)
Worsening azotemia/oliguria in severe progressive renal disease (discontinue)
Urinary retention from bladder outlet obstruction (prostatic hyperplasia, urethral narrowing)
Hypoproteinemia/nephrotic syndrome (reduced effect and potentiated ototoxicity)
Systemic lupus erythematosus (may be exacerbated or activated)
monitor: BOXED WARNING: ototoxicity - avoid high doses, rapid IV injection, and use in renal impairment/hypoproteinemia or with ototoxic drugs
Profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion - careful medical supervision required
Serum electrolytes (potassium, sodium, chloride, calcium, magnesium), CO2, BUN, creatinine
Blood pressure (orthostatic hypotension) and volume status / dehydration
Blood glucose in diabetics; serum uric acid (gout)

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Furosemide caused unexplained maternal deaths and abortions in rabbits at 2, 4, and 8 times the maximal recommended human dose, and animal studies showed fetal lethality and increased hydronephrosis in offspring. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus, and monitor fetal growth because of the potential for higher birth weights.
lact: Furosemide appears in breast milk, so caution should be exercised when administering it to a nursing mother. In addition, furosemide may inhibit lactation.
renal: Furosemide is predominantly excreted unchanged by the kidney. If increasing azotemia and oliguria occur during treatment of severe progressive renal disease, discontinue the drug. The risk of ototoxicity is increased in renal impairment, particularly with rapid IV injection or high doses, so avoid rapid administration and use controlled IV infusion for high parenteral doses. Reversible elevations of BUN may occur with dehydration and should be avoided; monitor renal function and electrolytes closely.
hepatic: In patients with hepatic cirrhosis and ascites, therapy is best initiated in the hospital. In hepatic coma and in states of electrolyte depletion, do not start furosemide until the basic condition is improved. Sudden alterations of fluid and electrolyte balance in cirrhotic patients may precipitate hepatic coma, so strict observation is necessary during diuresis; supplemental potassium chloride and, if needed, an aldosterone antagonist help prevent hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.

major: Aminoglycoside antibiotics - increased ototoxicity, especially in renal impairment; except in life-threatening situations, avoid the combination
Ethacrynic acid - do not use concomitantly due to ototoxicity risk
Cisplatin - increased risk of ototoxicity; cisplatin nephrotoxicity may be enhanced unless furosemide is given in lower doses with positive fluid balance
Lithium - reduced renal clearance of lithium with high risk of lithium toxicity; generally avoid with diuretics
ACE inhibitors / angiotensin II receptor blockers - severe hypotension and deterioration in renal function (including renal failure); may need to interrupt or reduce doses
Chloral hydrate - IV furosemide within 24 hours may cause flushing, sweating, restlessness, nausea, hypertension, and tachycardia; combination not recommended
moderate: Salicylates (high dose) - salicylate toxicity at lower doses via competition for renal excretion; ASA may transiently reduce creatinine clearance in chronic renal insufficiency
NSAIDs / indomethacin - reduced natriuretic and antihypertensive effect; reports of increased BUN, creatinine, potassium, and weight gain
Digitalis (digoxin) - hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia exaggerate digitalis toxicity, especially myocardial effects
Corticosteroids, ACTH, large amounts of licorice, prolonged laxative use - increased hypokalemia
Sucralfate - reduces natriuretic and antihypertensive effects; separate intake by at least 2 hours
Phenytoin - decreases intestinal absorption and lowers peak serum furosemide levels
Methotrexate and other renally secreted drugs - mutual reduction in clearance with elevated serum levels and potentiated toxicity
Cephalosporins - increased risk of cephalosporin-induced nephrotoxicity
Cyclosporine - increased risk of gouty arthritis from furosemide hyperuricemia plus cyclosporine urate retention
minor: Norepinephrine - decreased arterial responsiveness, though it remains effective
Ganglionic or peripheral adrenergic blocking drugs - potentiated hypotensive effect
High doses (>80 mg) may transiently alter thyroid hormone binding and total thyroid hormone levels
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; high-salt intake can blunt the diuretic effect.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol (and barbiturates or narcotics) may aggravate orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase blood glucose and alter glucose tolerance tests, raise serum uric acid, increase cholesterol/triglycerides, and lower serum calcium and magnesium; can affect urine glucose tests.

common: Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia)
serious: Ototoxicity - tinnitus and reversible or irreversible hearing loss/deafness (BOXED WARNING)
Profound diuresis with dehydration, blood volume reduction, and circulatory collapse
Hepatic encephalopathy in patients with hepatocellular insufficiency
Pancreatitis; intrahepatic cholestatic jaundice; increased liver enzymes
Interstitial nephritis; necrotizing angiitis; systemic vasculitis
Blood dyscrasias (thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, leukopenia, hemolytic anemia, eosinophilia)
rare: Precipitation of diabetes mellitus or gout
Nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis in premature infants and young children
emergency: Severe anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions (e.g., with shock)
Toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, erythema multiforme, DRESS, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
Circulatory collapse from severe volume/electrolyte depletion with possible thrombosis/embolism

monitoring: Serum electrolytes, particularly potassium, plus sodium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium - frequently in the first few months, then periodically
CO2, BUN, and creatinine; more frequent checks during vomiting or parenteral fluids
Blood pressure (including orthostatic) and signs of dehydration / volume depletion
Hearing / symptoms of ototoxicity (tinnitus) with high-dose or IV therapy
Blood and urine glucose in diabetics; serum uric acid
Renal function and renal ultrasonography in pediatric patients (nephrocalcinosis risk)
Watch for blood dyscrasias, liver or kidney damage
counsel: You may notice symptoms from losing too much fluid or salt, such as thirst, dry mouth, weakness, cramps, or dizziness - report these
Get up slowly from lying or sitting to reduce dizziness from low blood pressure
You may need potassium supplements or potassium-rich foods to prevent low potassium
Tell your doctor right away about ringing in the ears or any change in hearing
Your skin may be more sensitive to sunlight; use sun protection
If you have diabetes, this medicine can raise blood sugar and affect urine glucose tests
Tell your doctor if you are allergic to sulfa drugs
Avoid over-the-counter appetite suppressants and cold remedies that can raise blood pressure
pk: Oral diuresis within 1 hour; IV within minutes
Oral peak effect within the first or second hour
Store at 20 to 25 C; protect from light; dispense in light-resistant containers
pearls: BOXED WARNING: ototoxicity (tinnitus, reversible or irreversible hearing loss) is linked to rapid IV injection, high doses, renal impairment, hypoproteinemia, and concurrent ototoxic drugs - infuse high IV doses at <=4 mg/min
A potent diuretic: excessive dosing causes profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion, so individualize and supervise carefully
As a sulfonamide derivative, patients allergic to sulfonamides may also react to furosemide
Oral bioavailability is only about 64% of IV, so the IV dose is roughly half the oral dose for equivalent effect
Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia heighten digitalis toxicity - replete potassium and consider an aldosterone antagonist
Avoid combining with aminoglycosides or ethacrynic acid except when life-threatening; both compound ototoxicity
In cirrhosis/ascites, start in hospital - sudden electrolyte shifts can precipitate hepatic coma
Hemodialysis does not remove furosemide in overdose
missed: If you take furosemide on a schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the next dose, or taking it late would disrupt sleep with nighttime urination, skip the missed dose and resume your normal schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose produces dehydration, blood volume reduction, hypotension, and electrolyte imbalance with hypokalemia and hypochloremic alkalosis - extensions of the diuretic action. Treatment is supportive, centered on replacing excessive fluid and electrolyte losses; determine serum electrolytes, CO2 level, and blood pressure frequently. Ensure adequate drainage in patients with bladder outlet obstruction. Hemodialysis does not accelerate furosemide elimination.
